label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
First time posting here, though I've been reading this thread for a long time.

One of my blister pack patients passed away at the end of last month. I'll call her Mrs. H. Her daughter came in today to return the unused packs and her glucometer, and I've been thinking about it ever since I got home.

Mrs. H was in her eighties and had been coming to our store since 2019. Eleven medications, weekly blister pack, every Thursday. We're a small independent, just me and one tech, so you get to know your regulars. She lived alone after her husband died a few years ago, and she walked with a cane that had tennis balls on it.

Every Thursday she brought me something. Usually it was poppy seed cake. Once it was a jar of pickles that I honestly did not know what to do with. When it was Ramadan she remembered, without me saying anything. She wrapped the cake in foil, wrote my name on it, and told me not to eat it until sunset.

A few years ago a new doctor added a medication that interacted with her warfarin. I caught it and called him. I was only doing my job, the same thing any of you would do, but after that she told everybody I saved her life. I stopped trying to correct her.

Today her daughter gave me a card. Her mother wrote it a long time ago and for some reason never gave it to me. Inside it says "for my Arabic daughter."

I went to the back room and cried. My tech covered the counter for ten minutes.

School taught us pharmacology and interactions. Nobody taught us how to say goodbye to a patient. Nobody told us what to do when the daughter is standing at your counter with a bag of blister packs you filled yourself, with Thursday's still sealed.

My father was a pharmacist too, back in Egypt. He knew all the families. When I came to Canada I thought it would be different here, more professional distance, more just the prescription and the next person in line. It's not different.

I know we're not supposed to get attached. But you see someone every week for seven years. You know her medications better than her own family does. You notice when she looks tired and when her handwriting changes. I don't know how you do that and stay not attached, and I'm not sure I would want to be the pharmacist who can.

Next Thursday there will be no pack with her name on it, and I think that is when it will really hit me.

Does anyone else have a patient like this? I would like to hear about them.

---

To keep her unidentifiable, I left out the city and neighbourhood, the exact dates, her exact age, that she was Polish, and her daughter's and your tech's names. The last few lines about her handwriting, looking tired and next Thursday are my additions, so cut anything that isn't true for you.

reasons: The piece includes an identifying combination of Mrs. H’s medical history, routines, and personal details.
